newsitem.title: USA: McDonnell says Delta II launches to resume.
newsitem.headline: McDonnell says Delta II launches to resume.

text.p: McDonnell Douglas Corp said Thursday it expects launches of its Delta II rocket will resume around May 1.
McDonnell said it and the U.S. Air Force have been investigating the cause of an explosion of a Delta II rocket on the launch pad at Cape Canaveral Air Station in Florida.

"Currently, we would anticipate that launches would begin again on the program about May 1," McDonnell Douglas Chief Financial Officer James Palmer said on a teleconference. "We do anticipate that we would have a total of about 14 launches for the year."
He said the first launch would be for Iridium LLC, which is an international consortium of 17 companies and organizations including Motorola Inc, Sprint Corp, Lockheed Martin Corp and Raytheon Co.
Iridium is developing a satellite-based global wireless communications system.
Palmer said a Delta II launch in mid-May would be for another customer, which he did not identify.
McDonnell Douglas said accident-related costs and fewer launches from the Delta II failure contributed to lower first quarter earnings of $0.86 a share versus $0.89 a year ago.
"It does look like the program is back," Palmer said, referring to Delta II.
Palmer also said he expects McDonnell's proposed merger with Boeing Co would be completed around August 1.
He added that meetings for both McDonnell and Boeing shareholders would be held in mid-July to vote on the proposed merger.
"...(We) would anticipate that upon completion of the shareholder vote that the merger could be completed around the first of August or so," Palmer said.

Palmer said McDonnell and Boeing are both working to respond to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) request for additional information on the merger. In addition, both companies are gathering information to respond to any questions from the European Commission regarding the merger.
Palmer downplayed the FTC's request for additional information.
"It is a normal procedure for the FTC to (make)...a second request," he said. "So you should not view the second request as anything unusual in a transaction such as this."

He added he does not expect any significant antitrust issues to surface with regard to the proposed McDonnell-Boeing merger. "I think we're clearly complementary businesses between McDonnell Douglas and Boeing, and so I just don't see much issue on an antitrust perspective," Palmer said.
Regarding the 99-day strike at St. Louis operations, which was settled in September 1996, Palmer said the company has estimated increased costs through the second or third quarters.
Earlier, McDonnell said the phase-in of work after the strike impacted productivity in the first quarter.
